01.note: Rabbi Yehuda tells of Hyrcanus, son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who went out on Shabbat with a scarf on his shoulder and a thread of it tied around his finger so it would not fall. When the case came before the Sages, they said one may go out this way even without the thread tied to the finger. Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda taught in the name of Rav Hisda that this is the law.
01.why: The Gemara has been sorting ways of wearing cloth over the shoulders on Shabbat: a folded cloak counts as carrying, while runners may wear scarves. This incident settles that a scarf on the shoulder counts as worn even when it is not tied down.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: Son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus; he went out with a scarf on his shoulder on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus
people.about: Father of Hyrcanus.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda
people.about: Taught the ruling in the name of Rav Hisda.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage in whose name the final ruling is taught.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath. One of its prohibitions is carrying objects in a public area; clothing that is worn does not count as carried.
The binding Jewish law, as opposed to an opinion that was not accepted.

02.note: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once went out into a field with both sides of his cloak resting on his shoulders. Yehoshua ben Zeiruz, son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law, said to him: didn't Rabbi Meir hold one liable to a sin-offering for this? Rabbi asked whether Rabbi Meir was really that exacting, and lowered his cloak. Ravin gave another version: the man was Yehoshua ben Kefusai, Rabbi Akiva's son-in-law, citing Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi lowered his cloak. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda said the report was that Rabbi was asked about it, not that he wore it so.
02.why: The Gemara is working out which ways of folding and draping a garment on Shabbat count as wearing it and which count as carrying; here the top Sage of his day gives way at once to a stricter view he had not known.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he wore his cloak over his shoulders and lowered it when told of a stricter view.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Zeiruz
people.about: Son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law; in Rav Dimi's version, he raised the objection.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Kefusai
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's son-in-law; in Ravin's version, he raised the objection.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Brought the first version of the story from the Land of Israel to Babylonia.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: Brought a second version, naming a different questioner.

terms.meaning: A Temple sacrifice brought by someone who broke a serious law by mistake. Saying one is liable to it means the act counts as a real Shabbat violation.
Used alone as a name, it means Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, compiler of the Mishna.

03.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalled that when he and his fellow students learned Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and towels from the courtyard to the roof, and from the roof into an enclosure, until they reached the spring where they bathed. The Gemara adds the rulings of Shmuel and Rabbi Yohanan that one may dry oneself with a towel and carry it home.
03.why: Abaye asked Rav Yosef whether one may carry a towel home after bathing on Shabbat, and Rav Yosef named four authorities who allow it. The Gemara gives each one's source, and Rabbi's memory of Tekoa is his.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Tells of his student days, carrying towels to the spring.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's teacher in Tekoa; he allows carrying a towel home after drying off.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Ruled that one may dry off with a towel and carry it home.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Ruled the same, as reported by Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core code of Jewish law.
A fenced area, such as a yard, where carrying on Shabbat may be allowed, unlike a public street.

04.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh came to Phrygia and Deyomset, was drawn after their wine and baths, and forgot his learning. When he returned and stood to read from a Torah scroll, he meant to read 'This month shall be for you' but read 'Have their hearts become deaf', mixing up look-alike Hebrew letters. The Sages prayed for mercy on him, and his learning was restored.
04.why: Rabbi Helbo has just said that the wine of Phrygia and the waters of Deyomset cost Israel the ten tribes. This story shows the same pull on one great Sage, and the Gemara then ties it to Rabbi Nehorai's advice to go into exile to a place of Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh
people.about: A Sage who forgot his learning among the pleasures of Phrygia and Deyomset.

terms.meaning: A place of warm healing baths, mentioned alongside the wine region of Phrygia.
The handwritten scroll of the Five Books of Moses read aloud in the synagogue; it has no vowels, so the reader must know the text well.

05.note: Rabba bar bar Hana came to Pumbedita and did not attend Rav Yehuda's lecture. Rav Yehuda sent his attendant Adda to drag him there, and Adda did. Rabba bar bar Hana found Rav Yehuda teaching that one may not reset a broken bone on Shabbat, and told him that Rav Hana of Baghdad said in Shmuel's name that one may. Rav Yehuda answered: Hana is one of ours and Shmuel is one of ours, yet I had not heard this. Was I not right to drag you here?
05.why: The mishna forbids resetting a broken bone on Shabbat, and Shmuel rules that one may. The story shows that ruling arriving in Rav Yehuda's study hall, and the Gemara later uses it in a debate about a dislocated hand.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A visitor to Pumbedita, dragged to Rav Yehuda's lecture, who brought Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The teacher in Pumbedita whose lecture Rabba bar bar Hana skipped.

people.name: Adda
people.about: Rav Yehuda's attendant, sent to drag the visitor in.

people.name: Rav Hana of Baghdad
people.about: Reported Shmuel's ruling that a break may be reset on Shabbat.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose ruling permits resetting a broken bone on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: The binding Jewish law.
A Babylonian town with a major center of Torah study.

06.note: The Sages taught of a pious man whose field had a breach in its fence. He decided to fence it in, then remembered that it was Shabbat, so he held back and did not repair it. A miracle happened: a caper bush grew up in the gap, and from it came the livelihood of him and his household.
06.why: The mishna forbids waiting at the Shabbat boundary for nightfall in order to start weekday work, and the discussion has been about which weekday plans one may make or speak of on Shabbat. The pious man would not act even on a thought of work formed on Shabbat.

terms.meaning: A person who goes beyond what the law requires in serving God.
A thorny shrub whose buds and berries are eaten; here it closes the gap like a living fence.

07.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that a student of Rabbi Meir followed him into the bathhouse on Shabbat. The student wanted to rinse the floor, and Rabbi Meir told him one may not rinse. He wanted to smear the floor with oil, and Rabbi Meir told him one may not smear.
07.why: The mishna allows rinsing a corpse and smearing it with oil on Shabbat. The Gemara raises this incident as a challenge and answers that one floor can be confused with another, so the Sages forbade it, but a corpse cannot be confused with the ground.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Stopped his student from rinsing and oiling the bathhouse floor on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports the incident in the name of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is told.

08.note: Rabbi Hiyya told his wife: when a poor person comes, be quick to give him bread, so that others will be quick to give bread to your children. She said: are you cursing them? He answered that a verse is written, 'Due to this thing', and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that it means a wheel that turns in the world. The Gemara adds Rabbi Gamliel's teaching that whoever has compassion for others receives compassion from Heaven.
08.why: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar has just taught that poverty comes round to every family in time, reading the same verse as a turning wheel. Rabbi Hiyya puts that teaching into practice in his own home.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Tells his wife to give bread to the poor quickly.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya's wife
people.about: Asks whether he is cursing their children.

people.name: Rabbi Gamliel
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; taught that compassion for others brings compassion from Heaven.

terms.meaning: The students and tradition of the Sage Rabbi Yishmael, quoted as a source of teachings.

09.note: When Rabbi Hanina's daughter died, he did not cry over her. His wife said: have you just let a chicken out of your house? He answered: I would suffer twice, bereavement and blindness. The Gemara explains that he held the teaching of Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Ketzarta: there are six kinds of tears. Those from smoke, from crying, and from the bathroom are bad for the eyes; those from medicine, laughter, and sharp produce are good.
09.why: The Gemara is reading Ecclesiastes' picture of old age, and Shmuel has just said that after forty, tears no longer leave the eyesight unharmed. Rabbi Hanina's restraint shows a Sage living by that belief.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who did not cry when his daughter died.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina's wife
people.about: Rebukes him for not mourning their daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Taught the list of six kinds of tears.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Ketzarta
people.about: The Sage in whose name the teaching on tears is given.

10.note: A certain eunuch taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha, whose name sounds like the word for bald: how far is it to Karhina? He replied: as far as to Gozen, playing on the word for a castrated man. The eunuch: a bald buck sells for four. The rabbi: a castrated goat sells for eight. Seeing him barefoot, the eunuch said a man on a horse is a king, on a donkey a free man, in shoes at least a human being; one with none of these is better off buried. The rabbi answered: a beard is the glory of the face, a wife the joy of the heart, children the portion of the Lord; blessed is God who denied you all three. The eunuch: does a bald man quarrel? The rabbi: does a castrated goat rebuke?
10.why: The Gemara is gathering sayings around Ecclesiastes' picture of the aging body and has just quoted several aphorisms of the Sages; it follows them with this sharp exchange of insults.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha
people.about: A bald Sage who trades insults with a eunuch and wins.

people.name: the eunuch
people.about: An apostate who mocks the rabbi's baldness and bare feet.

terms.meaning: A castrated man, who could have no beard, wife or children, which is the point of the rabbi's reply.
Someone who has left the Jewish faith.

10.flag: The first STORY segment is a run of aphorisms about youth and old age (Rabbi Yosei bar Kisma, Rav Dimi, Shmuel to Rav Yehuda), separate from the eunuch exchange that follows.

11.note: Rav Yehuda taught that when a dead person has no one to mourn him, ten people should go and sit in his place. A man died in Rav Yehuda's neighborhood with no mourners, so every day of the seven days of mourning Rav Yehuda brought ten people to sit in the man's house. After seven days the dead man appeared to Rav Yehuda in a dream and said: put your mind at rest, for you have put my mind at rest.
11.why: Rav Hisda has just taught that a person's soul mourns for him all seven days after death; the story shows the dead are aware of those who mourn them, and Rabbi Abbahu goes on to say the dead know what is said before them.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Brought ten people each day to sit in mourning for a neighbor who had no mourners.

people.name: the dead man
people.about: A neighbor of Rav Yehuda with no mourners, who thanks him in a dream.

terms.meaning: Here, mourners: the family members who sit at home after a death and receive visitors who come to console them.
The first week of mourning after a burial, when mourners stay home and are visited.

12.note: Diggers working Rav Nahman's land were rebuked by Rav Ahai bar Yoshiya, who was buried there. They told Rav Nahman a man had rebuked them. Rav Nahman asked who he was; he said: Ahai bar Yoshiya. Rav Nahman asked: didn't Rav Mari say the righteous will turn to dust? Ahai: who is Mari, whom I do not know? Rav Nahman cited the verse 'And the dust returns to the earth'. Ahai answered that whoever taught him Ecclesiastes did not teach him Proverbs: 'envy is the rotting of the bones', so one without envy does not rot. Rav Nahman touched him, found him solid, and invited him into his house. Ahai said he had not read the Prophets either, citing 'when I open your graves'. To 'dust you are', Ahai replied it applies an hour before the resurrection.
12.why: Rav Mari has just said that even the bodies of the righteous will become dust. In this story a dead Sage, his body whole, argues back against that very statement.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The landowner who questions the dead man found on his land.

people.name: Rav Ahai bar Yoshiya
people.about: Buried in Rav Nahman's land; his body has not decayed, and he answers from the grave.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: The Sage who taught that the righteous turn to dust.

terms.meaning: Parts of the Hebrew Bible. Ahai mocks Rav Nahman for knowing one book but not the others.
The belief that God will one day bring the dead back to life.

13.note: Rabban Gamliel's donkey was loaded with honey on Shabbat, and he would not unload it until Shabbat was over. When Shabbat ended, the donkey died.
13.why: The mishna lets one take movable items off an animal on Shabbat, so the Gemara asks why Rabban Gamliel did not. It answers that the honey had spoiled, which made it off-limits to handle, and then asks why he let the animal suffer.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Would not unload his donkey's honey on Shabbat, and the donkey died.

14.note: Shmuel and the gentile sage Ablet were sitting and watching people go to the lake. Ablet said one man would not come back, because a snake would bite him and he would die. Shmuel said: if he is a Jew, he will go and come back. He went and came back. Ablet threw down the man's load and found inside a snake cut in two. Shmuel asked him what he had done. He said his group pooled bread every day; that day one of them had none and was embarrassed, so he offered to collect it and, at that man's turn, pretended to take from him. Shmuel said: you did a mitzva, and taught that 'charity saves from death' means even from death itself.
14.why: The Gemara is arguing that there is no constellation for the Jewish people: the fate written in the stars does not bind them. After deriving this from Abraham, it brings Shmuel's story as further proof.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who predicts the man will return, and draws the lesson about charity.

people.name: Ablet
people.about: A gentile sage who foretells the man's death by snakebite.

terms.meaning: The arrangement of stars and planets at a person's birth, believed by astrologers to fix his fate.
A commandment or good deed done in obedience to God.

15.note: Chaldean astrologers told Rabbi Akiva that on the day his daughter entered the wedding canopy, a snake would bite her and she would die. She worried greatly. That day she stuck her hair pin into the wall, and it happened to go into the eye of a snake. In the morning, when she pulled the pin out, the snake came out with it. Her father asked what she had done. She said a poor man had knocked at the door that evening while everyone was busy with the feast, and no one heard him, so she took her own portion and gave it to him. Rabbi Akiva said: you did a mitzva, and taught that 'charity saves from death' means even from death itself.
15.why: The Gemara is proving that there is no constellation for the Jewish people, that the stars' decree does not bind them; this is the next proof after Shmuel's story of the man saved from a snake.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The father, warned by astrologers about his daughter; he draws the lesson about charity.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva's daughter
people.about: Foretold to die on her wedding day; she is saved after giving her meal to a poor man.

terms.meaning: Astrologers; the name of an ancient people famous for reading the stars.
The canopy under which a Jewish wedding takes place; entering it means getting married.
A commandment or good deed done in obedience to God.

16.note: Chaldean astrologers told the mother of Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak that her son would be a thief. She never let him go with his head uncovered, telling him: cover your head so that the fear of Heaven will be upon you, and pray for mercy. He did not know why she said this. One day he was sitting and studying under a palm tree when his cloak fell off his head. He looked up, saw the palm tree, was overcome by his urge, climbed up and bit off a cluster of dates with his teeth.
16.why: This is the last of the Gemara's proofs that there is no constellation for the Jewish people, that fate in the stars does not bind them: the forecast came true only in the moment the head covering slipped.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage whose birth was said to mark him as a thief.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's mother
people.about: Kept her son's head covered after astrologers' warning.

terms.meaning: Astrologers; the name of an ancient people famous for reading the stars.
Awe of God; covering the head is a sign of it.

17.note: Rabbi Akiva picked the fruit of a citron tree on the first of the month of Shevat and set aside two different tithes from it: one following Beit Shammai, who count that day as the new year for trees, and one following Beit Hillel, who count it as still the old year.
17.why: Rav Sheizvi has said one may not take on two strict rulings that contradict each other. Rav Mesharshiya raises this incident against him, and the Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva was unsure which date Beit Hillel held, so he was strict both ways.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Set aside two tithes from one citron to satisfy both schools.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce that must be set aside. Which kind is due depends on the year of a seven-year cycle, so the date the fruit counts for matters.
A Hebrew month in mid-winter; the new year for trees falls in it.
Two early schools of Sages who disagreed on many laws.
A lemon-like fruit (etrog).

18.note: Rabbi Yitzhak told of an alleyway that ended at the sea on one side and at a refuse heap on the other. The case came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to rule whether one could carry in it on Shabbat, and he said nothing about it, neither permitting nor forbidding.
18.why: Rav Mesharshiya cites this case to prove that a yard owned by one person is treated differently from one owned by many. The Gemara explains Rabbi's silence by the worry that the heap might be cleared or the sea might pile up sand.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Heard the case of the alleyway and gave no ruling either way.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: Reported the incident, as Ravin bar Rav Adda relates.

terms.meaning: A side street shared by several houses. Carrying in it on Shabbat is allowed only if it is closed off properly.
A garbage pile; if tall enough it can act as a wall, but it may be cleared away.

19.note: A man from the valley of Beit Hortan stuck four poles into the four corners of his field and stretched a vine over them. The case came before the Sages, and they permitted it for the laws of diverse kinds, treating the field as enclosed. Reish Lakish said that just as they permitted it for diverse kinds, they permitted it for Shabbat. Rabbi Yohanan said they permitted it for diverse kinds but not for Shabbat.
19.why: The Gemara wants to show that Rabbi Yohanan agrees with Rav that a doorway-shaped frame does not close an opening wider than ten cubits; it argues that only such wide gaps explain his refusal for Shabbat.

people.name: a man from the valley of Beit Hortan
people.about: Fenced his field with four poles and a vine.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Held the Sages' permission applied to Shabbat too.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Held the permission applied only to diverse kinds, not to Shabbat.

terms.meaning: The Torah ban on planting certain crops together, such as grain next to a vineyard. A proper partition between them removes the problem.
Two upright poles with a crosspiece on top; in Jewish law it can count as a wall with an opening.

20.note: Rav Nahman built a doorway frame at the Exilarch's house following his own opinion, with the top reed not touching the side reeds. Rav Sheshet told his attendant Rav Gadda: go, pull them out and throw them away. He went, pulled them out and threw them away. The Exilarch's household found him and imprisoned him. Rav Sheshet went and stood at the door and called: Gadda, come out! And he came out and came to him.
20.why: Rav Nahman and Rav Sheshet have just disagreed over whether the side reeds of a doorway frame must touch the top reed for it to count; the story shows them acting out that dispute.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Built a doorway frame at the Exilarch's house by his own ruling.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Disagreed with Rav Nahman and had the frame torn down.

people.name: Rav Gadda
people.about: Rav Sheshet's attendant, who pulled out the reeds and was jailed for it.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, with his own court and household.
Two upright reeds with one across the top; in Jewish law it can count as a closed side, allowing carrying on Shabbat.
